## Recap: models, metrics, and units from Week 1 {.smaller}

- A probability forecast is **not yet a decision**; a threshold or loss rule
  turns probabilities into actions.
- A baseline is part of the scientific comparison, not a ceremonial model to
  discard.
- The unit of analysis matters: repeated views or labels of one case do not
  automatically create new independent cases.
- A metric summarizes performance only relative to a target and an evaluation
  population.

**Today:** what changes when the target itself is produced by repeated human
measurements?

## Vote first—no discussion yet {.smaller}

**1. Sentiment**

> “I waited only twenty minutes this time.”

Vote: **negative · neutral · positive**

**2. Factual truth**

> “The meeting is tomorrow.”

Vote: **true · false · cannot tell**

**3. Logical validity**

> All poets are writers. Some writers teach. Therefore, some poets teach.

Vote: **valid · invalid**

What, exactly, did our show of hands measure?

## A fixed category can hide variable judgments {.smaller}

A dataset may record one category $Y$. But if we repeat the measurement on the
same item $X=x$, the response can follow a distribution:

$$Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Categorical}\{q_1(x),\ldots,q_K(x)\}.$$

The response probabilities depend on:

- the item and its context;
- the construct, question, and instructions;
- the rater population or model.

An aggregation rule then turns a sample of responses into one reported category.

**Important:** this distribution describes judgments. A vote does not redefine
factual truth or logical validity—but it does reveal a measurement problem.

## DynaSent: five judgments per sentence {.smaller}

DynaSent is a benchmark for classifying English sentences as **negative,
neutral, or positive**. For every sentence $X=x$, it records

$$L_1,\ldots,L_n,\qquad n=5.$$

For a new judgment produced under the specified protocol, define the underlying
response probabilities

$$q_k(x)=P(L^\star=k\mid X=x),\qquad k\in\{-,0,+\}.$$

This $q(x)$ is the population quantity sometimes called the “true” proportion:
it is true **relative to the rater population and measurement protocol**.

We do not observe $q(x)$ directly.

::: notes
[Sources]
- Potts et al. (2021), DynaSent: https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.186/
:::

## Five observed labels estimate the response distribution {.smaller}

For class $k$, turn judgment $i$ into a zero-one indicator and average:

$$T_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{L_i=k\},\qquad
\widehat q_k(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}T_{ik},\quad n=5.$$

For example, five labels

$$(-,-,-,0,+)$$

give the empirical response proportions

$$\widehat q(x)=\left(\frac35,\frac15,\frac15\right).$$

Here $q(x)$ is the **underlying response distribution** and $\widehat q(x)$ is
the **observed five-rater distribution**—an estimate, not the same quantity.

::: notes
[Sources]
- Potts et al. (2021), DynaSent: https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.186/
:::

## First, hold the sentence fixed {.smaller}

Write response $i$ as

$$Y_i=f_i(X,U_i),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,$$

Here $X$ is the sentence; $U_i$ is everything else that can vary for response
$i$—rater, interpretation, attention, or model randomness.

$$X=x,\qquad Y_i=f_i(x,U_i).$$

Only the $U_i$'s vary. For two responses, the independence question is

$$Y_1\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_2\mid X=x\;?$$

> **Takeaway: Yes, under the stated model.** If $U_1\perp\!\!\!\perp U_2$ and
> no other shared input remains, then $Y_1\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_2\mid X=x$.
> Fixing $X$ removes only sentence-driven dependence.

## Now let the sentence vary {.smaller}

Draw one sentence, then collect every response:

$$X\sim P_X,\qquad Y_i=f_i(X,U_i).$$

Now $X$ varies too—and the same random $X$ enters every response:

$$
Y_1=f_1(X,U_1),\qquad Y_2=f_2(X,U_2).
$$

The marginal independence question is

$$Y_1\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_2\;?$$

> **Takeaway: Not necessarily.** Conditional independence can become marginal
> dependence because both responses vary with the same $X$. An ambiguous item,
> for example, can shift both response probabilities. Shared $X$ permits—but
> does not guarantee—dependence.

## Independence means factorization {.smaller}

**Within a fixed sentence**

$$
Y_1\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_2\mid X=x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{aligned}
&P(Y_1=y_1,Y_2=y_2\mid X=x)\\
&=P(Y_1=y_1\mid X=x)P(Y_2=y_2\mid X=x)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Across randomly drawn sentences**

$$
Y_1\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
P(Y_1=y_1,Y_2=y_2)=P(Y_1=y_1)P(Y_2=y_2).
$$

These are two definitions for two different probability models. One
factorization does not imply the other.

## Covariance measures association {.smaller}

For a chosen class $k$, use numeric indicators

$$Y_i=\mathbf 1\{L_i=k\},\qquad i=1,2.$$

Covariance measures whether two centered numeric responses tend to have the same
sign:

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)
=E\!\left[(Y_1-E[Y_1])(Y_2-E[Y_2])\right].
$$

- **positive:** the responses tend to be above or below their means together;
- **zero:** the centered product has expected value zero;
- **negative:** one tends to be above its mean when the other is below.

Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance is weaker than
independence in general.

## Center each response within and between sentences {.smaller}

To identify two sources of covariance, add and subtract the conditional mean:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_1-E[Y_1]
&=\underbrace{Y_1-E[Y_1\mid X]}_{\text{within-sentence residual}}\\
&\quad+\underbrace{E[Y_1\mid X]-E[Y_1]}_{\text{between-sentence shift}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_2-E[Y_2]
&=\underbrace{Y_2-E[Y_2\mid X]}_{\text{within-sentence residual}}\\
&\quad+\underbrace{E[Y_2\mid X]-E[Y_2]}_{\text{between-sentence shift}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Why the covariance decomposition works {.smaller}

Multiply the two centered-response decompositions and take expected values. The
two cross-products disappear because conditional residuals have conditional
expected value zero:

$$E[Y_i-E[Y_i\mid X]\mid X]=0,\qquad i=1,2.$$

What remains is **within-sentence covariance + between-sentence covariance**.

## The law of total covariance keeps the questions straight {.smaller}

For two measurements $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ made on a shared random sentence $X$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)
=\underbrace{E\!\left[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2\mid X)\right]}_{\text{average within-sentence covariance}}
+\underbrace{\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(E[Y_1\mid X],E[Y_2\mid X]\right)}_{\text{association across sentences}}.
$$

The left side is marginal covariance over randomly drawn sentences. The two
terms on the right describe two distinct sources of association.

::: notes
[Sources]
- Law of total covariance: https://statproofbook.github.io/P/cov-tot
:::

## Within-sentence covariance is zero under conditional independence {.smaller}

$$E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2\mid X)]$$

The term is exactly zero when the **average conditional covariance** is zero:

$$E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2\mid X)]=0.$$

A stronger, easier-to-interpret condition is

$$\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2\mid X=x)=0\quad\text{for every }x.$$

Conditional independence is sufficient for this:

$$Y_1\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_2\mid X,$$

but the reverse is not generally true: zero covariance is weaker than
independence.

## Within-sentence covariance can remain after fixing the sentence {.smaller}

$$E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2\mid X)]\ne0$$

requires systematic positive or negative covariance **within fixed sentences**.

For example:

- one rater sees or discusses the other's answer;
- both raters receive the same extra hint for that item;
- one reported response is constructed using the other response.

> **Takeaway:** sentence difficulty cannot explain this within-sentence
> covariance because the sentence has already been held fixed. Look for another
> shared part of the measurement process.

## Across-sentence covariance is zero when probabilities are unassociated {.smaller}

Because $Y_i=\mathbf1\{L_i=k\}$, define

$$m_i(x)=E[Y_i\mid X=x]=P(L_i=k\mid X=x).$$

The across-sentence part is

$$\operatorname{Cov}(m_1(X),m_2(X)).$$

**Concrete zero case:** draw either sentence type with equal probability.

| Sentence type $X$ | $m_1(X)$ | $m_2(X)$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| clearly positive | 0.9 | 0.5 |
| clearly negative | 0.1 | 0.5 |

Rater 1's probability changes, but rater 2's does not:

$$\operatorname{Cov}(m_1(X),m_2(X))=0.$$

More generally, this covariance is zero whenever the centered product averages
to zero. Either $m_i(x)$ being constant is an easy sufficient condition.

## Across-sentence covariance is nonzero when probabilities change together {.smaller}

Draw one of two sentence types with equal probability. Two raters work
independently conditional on the type.

| Sentence type $X$ | $m_1(X)$ | $m_2(X)$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| clearly positive | 0.9 | 0.9 |
| clearly negative | 0.1 | 0.1 |

The total-covariance identity gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Within sentences:}\quad
E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2\mid X)]
&=0,\\
\text{Across sentences:}\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(m_1(X),m_2(X))
&=0.16,\\[2mm]
\text{Total:}\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)&=0+0.16=0.16.
\end{aligned}
$$

Within sentences, independence makes the first piece zero. Across sentences,
the probabilities change together. Thus the responses are marginally dependent
entirely because the sentence varies.

## Two covariance questions give four cases {.smaller}

::: {.fragment}
- **Within a fixed sentence:** are the two responses still associated?
- **Across sentences:** do both raters tend to call the same sentences positive?
:::

::: {.fragment}
| | **Across sentences: $0$** | **Across sentences: $\ne0$** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Within sentences: $0$** | Independent raters;<br>no sentence pattern | Independent raters;<br>shared sentence pattern |
| **Within sentences: $\ne0$** | Shared cue;<br>no sentence pattern | Shared cue;<br>shared sentence pattern |
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Shared sentence pattern:** both raters are more likely to say positive for the
same kinds of sentences.
:::

## Independent raters can show either pattern {.smaller .compact-table}

Let $Y_i=1$ when rater $i$ says **positive**. Draw A or B with equal probability:

> **A:** “The staff were kind and solved my problem.”  
> **B:** “The staff were rude and ignored me.”

| Rater behavior | A: $(m_1,m_2)$ | B: $(m_1,m_2)$ | Within | Across |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Use sentence sentiment independently | $(.9,.9)$ | $(.1,.1)$ | $0$ | $>0$ |
| Flip fair coins independently | $(.5,.5)$ | $(.5,.5)$ | $0$ | $0$ |

**First row:** both probabilities are high for A and low for B.  
**Second row:** neither probability changes with the sentence.

## A shared cue gives the two bottom-row patterns {.smaller .compact-table}

Now both raters receive the same randomly assigned cue—**“lean positive”** or
**“lean negative”**—before answering. The cue links their responses even after
we fix the sentence, so the within-sentence covariance is nonzero.

| How the cue is used | $m_1(A),m_2(A)$ | $m_1(B),m_2(B)$ | Within | Across |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Cue overrides the sentence | $(.5,.5)$ | $(.5,.5)$ | $\ne0$ | $0$ |
| Cue nudges, but sentiment still matters | $(.8,.8)$ | $(.2,.2)$ | $\ne0$ | $>0$ |

The shared cue explains the **within-sentence** association. Sentence A versus
B explains the additional **across-sentence** association in the second row.

## Frozen-model covariance comes from changing sentences {.smaller}

For a fixed sentence $X=x$, the outputs $f_1(x)$ and $f_2(x)$ are constants:

$$\operatorname{Cov}(f_1(X),f_2(X)\mid X=x)=0.$$

::: {.fragment}
For a random sentence $X$, both outputs change with the sentence, so
$\operatorname{Cov}(f_1(X),f_2(X))$ can be nonzero.

**Point:** frozen models have no repeated-response randomness after $X$ is
fixed. Any covariance is **across sentences**.
:::

## Independent does not mean interchangeable {.smaller .compact-table}

**Independent:** knowing rater 1's answer does not change the distribution of
rater 2's answer.

**Exchangeable:** swapping the rater names does not change the joint
distribution.

| Fixed-sentence example | Independent? | Exchangeable? |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Expert and novice work separately but have different response probabilities | Yes | No |
| Identical raters receive the same random cue | No | Yes |

These are different modeling claims; neither implies the other.

## Averaging labels does not erase dependence {.smaller}

The observed class-$k$ proportion is

$$\widehat q_k=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^mT_{ik}.$$

Its conditional variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat q_k\mid X=x)
=\frac{1}{m^2}\Bigg[&\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(T_{ik}\mid x)\\
&+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(T_{ik},T_{jk}\mid x)\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
$$

**Takeaway:** positive covariance limits how much averaging reduces variance.

## Conditional iid is what gives the $1/m$ variance {.smaller}

For one class $k$, let
$T_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{\text{rater }i\text{ chooses }k\}$.

The conditional iid model is

$$
T_{1k},\ldots,T_{mk}\mid X=x
\ \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\
\operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(q_k(x)\right).
$$

It gives

$$
E[\widehat q_k\mid x]=q_k(x),\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat q_k\mid x)
=\frac{q_k(x)(1-q_k(x))}{m}.
$$

> **Point:** the familiar $1/m$ reduction is a consequence of the conditional
> iid model—not a consequence of averaging alone.

## Break

### Stretch. Breathe. Argue about whether “fine” is positive or neutral.

When we return: **How should we score a probability forecast when labels can
vary?**

## Why score the full probability forecast? {.smaller}

A model reports a distribution, not just a winning class:

$$p=(0.60,\ 0.30,\ 0.10),$$

- Accuracy treats $0.51$ and $0.99$ alike when they predict the same class.
- Confident mistakes should cost more than cautious mistakes.
- We may compare the forecast with a hard label or observed rater proportions.

**Brier score compares the full forecast with a chosen target.**

## Brier score is squared distance from the chosen target {.smaller}

**Homework 2, Problem 1:** you will derive the expected value of this score.

For DynaSent's three classes, let $p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ be the forecast and
$t=(t_1,t_2,t_3)$ the chosen target. Then

$$B(p,t)=\sum_{k=1}^3(p_k-t_k)^2.$$

::: {.fragment}
$$B(p,t)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=t.$$
Larger values mean the forecast is farther from the target.
:::

::: {.fragment}
One realized score measures the **total discrepancy**. It cannot tell whether
that discrepancy came from forecast mismatch, label variability, or how the
target was constructed.
:::

Expected Brier score separates the first two.

## Expected Brier score exposes label variability {.smaller}

Fix a sentence $X=x$. Let $T$ be one random one-hot label and define

$$q_k(x)=P(T_k=1\mid X=x)=E[T_k\mid X=x].$$

For a fixed forecast $p$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[B(p,T)\mid x]
&=\sum_k E[(p_k-T_k)^2\mid x]\\
&=\underbrace{\sum_k(p_k-q_k)^2}_{\text{forecast mismatch}}
+\underbrace{\sum_k q_k(1-q_k)}_{\text{label variability}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The cross term vanishes because $E[T_k-q_k\mid x]=0$.

::: notes
[Sources]
- Bishop & Bishop, *Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts*, Chapter 5 and Exercise 5.1.
:::

## Label variability is largest when responses are evenly split {.smaller .compact-table}

$$\sum_k q_k(1-q_k)=1-\sum_k q_k^2.$$

| Response distribution $q$ | Variability | Meaning |
|:---:|:---:|---|
| $(1,0,0)$ | $0$ | Every repeated label is the same. |
| $(0.8,0.2,0)$ | $0.32$ | Labels sometimes disagree. |
| $(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ | $2/3$ | Responses are evenly split. |

Even when $p=q$, the expected score is not generally zero: a newly generated
label can still differ from the response distribution.

## Averaging shrinks label variability by $1/m$ {.smaller}

For $\widehat q=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mT_i$, the conditional iid model gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[B(p,\widehat q)\mid x]
&=\sum_k(p_k-q_k)^2
&&\text{forecast mismatch}\\[2mm]
&\quad+\frac{1}{m}\sum_kq_k(1-q_k)
&&\text{label variability}.
\end{aligned}
$$

**Only the label-variability term shrinks; forecast mismatch is unchanged.**

## Dependence changes how much averaging buys us {.smaller}

Without conditional independence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat q_k\mid x)
&=\frac{1}{m^2}\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(T_{ik}\mid x)\\
&\quad+\frac{2}{m^2}\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(T_{ik},T_{jk}\mid x).
\end{aligned}
$$

Positive covariance leaves more variability in the average than the iid formula
predicts. Negative covariance leaves less.

Therefore a soft-target Brier score is not “variability free.” Its expected
variability depends on the rater design.

## Hard and soft targets preserve different information {.smaller}

Five votes $(4,1,0)$ in negative, neutral, positive order give

$$t_{\text{hard}}=(1,0,0),\qquad
t_{\text{soft}}=(0.8,0.2,0).$$

**Hard target:** keeps only the majority class; the neutral vote disappears.

**Soft target:** keeps all five vote fractions; it still reflects only five
measurements.

Neither is literal ground truth. Comparing both scores shows how much the
evaluation depends on the target choice.

## What we did today {.smaller}

1. **Independence needs a repeated experiment:** say what is held fixed and
   what is redrawn.
2. **Dependence has two sources:** association within a sentence and across
   changing sentences.
3. **A shared sentence permits marginal dependence; it does not guarantee it.**
4. **Expected Brier score separates** forecast mismatch from label variability.
5. **The $1/m$ reduction requires conditional iid raters.** Dependence changes
   how much averaging helps.
